title: Quantum Monte Carlo in the Age of Many-Body Quantum Information
authors: Yi-Ming Ding, Bin-Bin Mao, Zheng Yan
abstract: Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods are among the central numerical tools for studying strongly correlated quantum many-body systems, particularly in higher dimensions. As quantum information has introduced new information-theoretic perspectives and diagnostics into many-body physics, QMC methods have accordingly been extended beyond the measurement of conventional linear observables. This review summarizes recent progress in adapting QMC to many-body quantum-information, focusing on qubit or spin-$1/2$ systems as a concrete setting while keeping the discussion broadly applicable to qudit and bosonic systems. We present a unified perspective on the extraction of nonlinear diagnostics, including entanglement entropies and entanglement spectra, Rényi negativities for mixed-state entanglement, stabilizer entropies for quantum magic, and decoherence-driven phenomena such as the interplay between imaginary-time evolution and decoherence and strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking.
summary: This review summarizes how Quantum Monte Carlo methods can be adapted to calculate complex, nonlinear quantum information diagnostics for many-body systems. It moves beyond simple expectation values to compute measures like entanglement entropy by sampling the full density matrix structure. This work is crucial for advancing the study of quantum correlations in strongly correlated materials using powerful numerical tools.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of extending Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods beyond calculating conventional linear observables to compute complex, nonlinear diagnostics from many-body quantum information theory.
main_result: It provides a unified perspective on adapting QMC to extract advanced quantum information measures, such as entanglement entropies and entanglement spectra, for strongly correlated systems.
method: The review details various QMC formulations, including those based on generalized partition-function ratios, allowing access to off-diagonal density matrix elements necessary for entanglement diagnostics.
model_or_system: The focus is on strongly correlated quantum many-body systems, using qubit or spin-1/2 systems as the primary concrete setting, though the discussion is broadly applicable to qudit and bosonic systems.
key_observables: Entanglement entropies, entanglement spectra, Rényi negativities, stabilizer entropies, and observables related to spontaneous symmetry breaking.
important_parameters: The primary limitation discussed is the sign problem, which restricts the applicability of QMC methods.
main_assumptions: The review assumes that the physical systems under consideration admit sign-problem-free QMC representations for the desired observables.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the mathematical difference between calculating the trace of a density matrix (full configuration space) versus calculating an open-time-boundary matrix element, highlighting the need to close boundary indices.
paper_structure: The discussion is organized logically by state representations (Section II), choice of basis (Section III), and general ratio estimation techniques (Section IV) to build a comprehensive methodological guide.
why_interesting: It is highly relevant as it bridges advanced numerical techniques (QMC) with cutting-edge diagnostics in quantum information (entanglement measures), providing a roadmap for future simulations in AMO physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Diagrammatic illustration of a density matrix and its trace. (a) An open-time-boundary matrix element ⟨s|˜ρ|s′⟩, where ˜ρ connects the ket boundary state |s′⟩to the bra boundary state ⟨s| along the transfer direction. (b) The trace Tr(˜ρ), obtained by identifying s = s′, closing the boundary legs, and summing over the common boundary state. Only the boundary states are shown explicitly; representation-dependent auxiliary variables, such as SSE operator strings or path-integral imaginary-time histories, are omitted.

FIG. 2: Diagrammatic illustration of a RDM and its trace. (a) The matrix element ⟨sA|˜ρA|s′ A⟩is obtained by identifying and summing over the B boundary states of the full density matrix, while keeping the A boundary states open. (b) Taking TrA(˜ρA) further identifies and sums over the remaining A boundary states, closing all boundary legs and giving TrA(˜ρA) = Tr(˜ρ).

FIG. 3: Diagrammatic illustration of the replicated RDM ˜ρ2 A and its trace. (a) The open-boundary matrix element of ˜ρ2 A. The two replicas are glued sequentially in subsystem A: the ket boundary state |s(1) A ′⟩of the first replica is identified with the bra boundary state ⟨s(2) A | of the second. The B degrees of freedom are traced within each replica. (b) The trace TrA(˜ρ2 A), obtained by further identifying and summing over the remaining open A boundary states |s(2) A ′⟩and ⟨s(1) A |. This closes all A boundary legs.

FIG. 4: Diagrammatic illustration of the partially transposed replicated partition function Tr[(˜ρTB AB)3]. The three replicas are glued cyclically in subsystem A, as in the ordinary replicated construction. In subsystem B, however, the partial transpose changes the boundary connectivity, producing a different gluing pattern between replicas.

FIG. 5: Diagrammatic illustration of the operator-inserted partition function ZO = Tr(˜ρO). The upper replica represents the operator insertion O, while the lower replica represents the density matrix ˜ρ. Closing the boundary indices implements the trace.
